newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM says may ease up on spending cut target.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM says may ease up on spending cut target.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, indicating a possible compromise with communist opponents in parliament, said his government may be able to ease up on drastic planned spending cuts.

Quoted by Itar-Tass news agency, Chernomyrdin said on Friday night that he was looking for new sources of revenue that might allow the government to scale back the 108 trillion roubles ($19 billion) of spending cuts it will ask parliament to approve next week.

"The stated sum of 108 trillion roubles, by which it is planned to reduce the expenditure part of the budget, could be changed, as the government is now searching for additional means of financing," the premier told reporters in St Petersburg.
A shortfall in tax revenue of up to 50 percent in the first quarter prompted ministers to slash spending under the 1997 budget by one-fifth.
The communist speaker of the State Duma lower house said last week this was too much and urged a compromise.
Noting that the government had yet to define all the cuts, Chernomyrdin was quoted as saying: "The overall sum itself could be changed in the direction of a reduction."

Chernomyrdin is due to report to parliament on the first quarter budget performance on May 21. His first deputy, Anatoly Chubais, a particular hate-figure for the communists, will present the cuts, or sequestration plan.
Both ministers can expect a rough ride. The Duma will vote on the scheme two days later. Its budget committee has already said it will recommend rejecting the scheme as it stands.

The depth of the government's budget crisis was highlighted on Friday when the minority Yabloko liberal party, which has no sympathy for the communists' alternative scheme to simply print money, started the process for a no-confidence vote.
The motion has virtually no chance of success but underlined the extent of opposition to cutting spending when millions of Russians are living on the breadline.
Many workers and pensioners have not been paid for months and institutions, including schools, hospitals and the armed forces, are desperately short of cash.
Yabloko leader Grigory Yavlinsky criticised the government for failing to present any plans for increasing revenue.
Government officials have said there are other ways of cutting spending even if parliament rejects the sequestration.

The government, formed two months ago when President Boris Yeltsin appointed Chubais and a number of other young reformers to senior posts, has made increasing tax revenues a priority for its 1998 budget.
Yeltsin has accused big companies, particularly in the oil and gas sector, of failing to contribute fully.

Last week, the government in the shape of 37-year-old First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, took steps to reassert its control over Gazprom, the vast natural gas monopoly once headed by Chernomyrdin.
The state has a 40 percent stake but, Nemtsov says, made only $3.5 million out of it in the past two years.
